1. The possible hypothesis: se + congiuntivo imperfetto + conditional
When you talk about something imaginary, unlikely or impossible NOW ("if I had time…"), Italian uses SE + CONGIUNTIVO IMPERFETTO and the present conditional in the main clause:
If I had time, I'd sleep.
If I were rich, I'd buy a villa.
If Viola slept, we'd be happy.
If I could sing, I'd sing for her.

Romanian puts the conditional in BOTH parts ("dacă AȘ AVEA, AȘ DORMI"). Italian does NOT: after "se" comes the congiuntivo imperfetto (like English "if I HAD", not "if I would have"). "Se AVESSI tempo", NOT "Se avrei tempo". "Se avrei" is the mistake Italians tease each other about!
The "se" clause can go at the beginning or the end. The forms stay the same:
I'd be happy if she slept for three hours.
Se Viola dorme, dormiamo anche noi.
Se Viola dormisse, dormiremmo anche noi.
The same situation can be expressed both ways. The difference is how likely it seems to you: "Se vinco, …" (I think I can win) / "Se vincessi, …" (I'm dreaming).
The expression "se fossi in te / in lei / in voi" (if I were you) is the most polite way to give advice:
If I were you, I'd call the doctor.
I wouldn't do it, if I were you.
"Al posto tuo" (in your place) + conditional is another, shorter option: "Al posto tuo dormirei."
Don't swap the forms: NOT "se sarei", NOT "fossi felice se dormirebbe". Subjunctive after "se", conditional in the other part.
If I were you, I'd go to bed.
I'd come every week if I lived closer.
If we were in Sibiu, Grandma would help us.
Real hypothesis: "If it rains, we'll stay at home."

No book had prepared them for the nights. Viola slept all day, as peaceful as one of Botticelli's angels, and at eleven at night she would open her eyes, look at the ceiling with interest and start to cry. She cried until three, until four, sometimes until dawn. "If she had a switch," Matei would say, "I'd find it and turn it off."

Everyone had advice. Graziella said: "If I were you, I'd give her a little camomile." Rosaria phoned from Naples every evening: "If you took her for a drive, she'd fall asleep at once. Gennaro only slept in the car." Grandma Assunta, on the phone, just said: "If it were my problem, I'd take her to Naples. No child cries there, because there's too much noise to hear it."

Pietro had an idea too. He turned up one morning with his old music player. "If you played her the Batman soundtrack, she'd sleep for sure. It worked with me." They tried it, so as not to offend him. Viola listened to the music with a very serious expression, then cried harder than before. "Maybe she prefers Superman," Pietro concluded, disappointed.

Even Bellini had an opinion. One day he left a book called "The Newborn's Sleep" on Matei's table, with a note: "If you read it, perhaps you'd understand something. I haven't read it, having no children. But the cover is nice." Matei read it in three nights while he rocked Viola. The book said that every baby is different. Matei thought that if he'd known that before, he'd have saved twenty euros.

After two weeks Matei went back to the workshop. On the first day he fell asleep at eleven in the morning, with his head on the table, next to a fourteenth-century Madonna. When he woke up, two hours later, there was a blanket over his shoulders and the professor was working quietly on the other side of the room. "If I'd woken you," Bellini said without turning round, "your wife would never have forgiven me. And I'm afraid of your wife."

Doina had stayed in Florence to help them. Ion had gone back to Sibiu after a week, because Lupu the dog wouldn't eat without him. Doina, on the other hand, had decided to stay a month. She spoke almost no Italian, but she didn't need to. She changed nappies, gave the baby her bath, cooked for three and, above all, sent Matei and Giulia to bed. "If you don't sleep," she would say in Romanian, "who will look after her when I've gone?"

One night, at about three, Matei woke up and heard nothing. No crying. He got up, worried, and went to the nursery. The door was ajar. Doina was sitting in the rocking chair with Viola in her arms, singing softly, almost in a whisper, a song in Romanian. Viola was looking at her with her eyes open, calm, as if she were listening to a story.

Matei stopped in the doorway. He knew that song. He didn't know how, he didn't know where from, but he knew it. The words came back to him one after another, as if someone were writing them in the air. "Mum," he whispered. "What song is that?" Doina looked up. "It's your grandmother Viorica's lullaby. She sang it to me when I was little. And she sang it to you when you were two or three. Don't you remember?"

Matei sat down on the floor next to the rocking chair. "I only remembered her hands and a song," he said. "But I thought the song was a dream." Doina smiled. "It wasn't a dream. If your grandmother were here, she'd sing it better than me. She had a beautiful voice. You, unfortunately, got your father's voice." Matei laughed quietly, so as not to wake Viola, who had fallen asleep.

Over the next few days Doina taught him all the words. Matei wrote them on a sheet of paper and learned them by heart, the way he used to learn the names of pigments at university. He sang terribly. Giulia said that if the neighbours heard him, they'd call the police. But when he sang, Viola stopped crying and looked at him with her big dark eyes, as if she recognised him.

On her last evening before leaving, Doina made sarmale for the whole of via Maggio. Graziella brought tiramisù, Signor Franco a bottle of wine, Pietro his music player, "just in case". At the end of the dinner Doina hugged Giulia and said, in her Italian of very few words: "If I lived closer, I'd come every week." Giulia held her tight. "If you lived closer," she replied, "we'd never let you go home again."

That night Viola slept for five hours in a row. For the first time. Matei and Giulia woke at four, frightened by the silence, and ran to the nursery. Viola was sleeping, with one little fist tucked under her cheek. On the bedside table, next to the cot, Doina had left the sheet with the words of the song, and underneath she had written: "For Viola, from her great-grandmother Viorica."
